name: Babylonian Chronicle tablet BM 21946 (ABC 5)
findspot_description: Unprovenanced: purchased from a dealer in 1896; original excavation unknown.
description: Chronicle covering Nebuchadnezzar II's first eleven years: Carchemish (605), the accession, Levantine campaigns, and the capture of "the city of Judah" (597). Date of writing given as c. 595 BC by Wikipedia.

name: Jehoiachin's ration tablets (Babylon)
findspot_description: Vaulted building near the Ishtar Gate, Babylon (Koldewey excavations).
description: Oil ration lists naming Ya'u-kīnu, king of the land of Yahudu, and his sons among foreign recipients at the Babylonian court.

name: East India House Inscription
findspot_description: Ruins of Babylon; unearthed before 1803 by Sir Harford Jones Brydges.
description: Foundation inscription of Nebuchadnezzar II describing his temple building and devotion to the shrines of Babylon and Borsippa.

name: Cyrus Cylinder
findspot_description: Babylon, found by Hormuzd Rassam in March 1879; the article places it in the Esagila foundations, though Rassam gave conflicting locations.
description: Akkadian building inscription of Cyrus II proclaiming that Marduk let him enter Babylon without battle and denouncing Nabonidus.

name: Thiele (1983) divided-monarchy chronology
description: E. R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings, 3rd ed. Uses coregencies and differing regnal reckonings.

name: Albright (1945) divided-monarchy chronology
description: W. F. Albright, BASOR 100 (1945).

name: Septuagint (Greek) dates in Daniel
description: Dates found in Greek witnesses but absent from the Masoretic/Aramaic text. Kept separate so textual traditions are never mixed (SPEC 12.6).

name: Belshazzar's years counted from the entrusting of the kingship
description: Daniel dates visions to Belshazzar's first and third years (7:1; 8:1), but no Babylonian document counts years of Belshazzar. This model assumes Daniel counts from the moment Nabonidus "entrusted the kingship" to him (Verse Account ii), which the Chronicle and Smith (via Dougherty) place around Nabonidus's 3rd year. Outside this model the visions are left undated.

name: Fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (accession-year count of Nebuchadnezzar's years)
description: Counts "the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar" (2 Kgs 25:8) in the Babylonian way, with an accession year: year 19 = Nisan 586 – Nisan 585, so the Temple burned in Ab 586. Associated with E. R. Thiele (as reported by Young 2004).

name: Fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC (non-accession count of Nebuchadnezzar's years in 2 Kings)
description: Counts Nebuchadnezzar's years in 2 Kings without an accession year (year 1 = 605/604), so year 19 = Nisan 587 – Nisan 586 and the Temple burned in Ab 587; the "eighth year" of 2 Kgs 24:12 then matches the chronicle's Adar of year 7 (March 597). R. C. Young (2004), with Wiseman and Kitchen.

name: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3 (Fall of Nineveh Chronicle)
Berossus, Babyloniaca (fragments)
description: History of Babylonia by the Babylonian priest Berossus, written in Greek c. 290–280 BC; survives only in quotations.

name: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men (Greek additions to Daniel 3)
document_type: Deuterocanonical addition (non-canonical in the Protestant canon)
description: Prayer and hymn inserted after Dan 3:23 in Greek Daniel. Indexed as a textual source only (SPEC 5.6), not as Scripture of the 66-book canon.

name: Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242)
description: Fragmentary first-person account of Nabonidus afflicted for seven years at Tayma and healed by God, with a Judean urging public acknowledgement. Manuscript dated c. 75–25 BC; composition date disputed.

name: Nabonidus Cylinder from Ur
description: Foundation text for the ziggurat of Sin at Ur, found by J. G. Taylor in 1854 (four cylinders); ends with a prayer for Belshazzar, the eldest son. Museum numbers not verified.

name: Verse Account of Nabonidus
description: Hostile account of Nabonidus's reign: he entrusts the kingship to his eldest son, goes to Tayma, and is replaced by the pious Cyrus.

name: Behistun inscription of Darius I
document_type: Royal rock inscription (trilingual: Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian)
description: Darius I's account of his accession and the revolts of his first years, with a list of 23 subject lands (§6).

name: 1 Enoch, Book of Parables (Similitudes), chs. 37–71
description: Visions of the Head of Days and the Son of Man; date disputed (Charles: c. 105–64 BC; others later).

name: 2 Esdras (4 Ezra)
description: Apocalypse attributed to Ezra; its eagle vision (chs. 11–12) reinterprets Daniel's fourth kingdom as Rome, and ch. 13 has a man rising from the sea with the clouds. Dated by Driver "probably under Domitian" (AD 81–96).

name: Kingdom of Judah
description: Southern Israelite kingdom with its capital at Jerusalem.

name: Kingdom of Israel (Northern Kingdom)
description: Northern Israelite kingdom with its capital at Samaria.

name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
description: Babylonian empire of the Chaldean dynasty, from Nabopolassar (626 BC) to the fall of Babylon (539 BC).

name: Egypt (Twenty-sixth Dynasty)
description: Saite dynasty of Egypt, including Necho II.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
description: Persian empire founded by Cyrus II.

name: Median kingdom (Media)
description: Iranian kingdom centred on Ecbatana; its last king Astyages was defeated by Cyrus (ABC 7 ii 1–4, year 6 of Nabonidus).

name: Macedonian empire of Alexander the Great
description: The empire of Alexander III of Macedon (336–323 BC), divided among his successors after his death.

name: Seleucid empire
description: Hellenistic kingdom founded by Seleucus I (era from 312/311 BC), ruling Syria and Mesopotamia; Antiochus IV Epiphanes reigned 175–164 BC.

name: Rome (Republic and Empire)
description: The Roman state, republic and empire; identified with Daniel's fourth kingdom in the traditional Christian reading.

name: Ptolemaic kingdom (Egypt)
description: The Macedonian dynasty founded in Egypt by Ptolemy son of Lagus after Alexander's death (323 BC), ending with Cleopatra VII (30 BC). Most interpreters read it as Daniel 11's "king of the south".

description: Biblical name for the land of Babylonia (Dan 1:2). No coordinates are recorded for a region.

hypotheses.label: Near the mound of Dowair/Duair, south-east of Babylon (Oppert, 19th c.)
hypotheses.reasoning: A pedestal of a huge statue was reported on the mound. 19th-century report, not verified by modern publication; no sourced coordinates.

hypotheses.label: A tract a little south of Tekrit on the Tigris ("Dur")
proponents: Unnamed proposers in Smith's Bible Dictionary
hypotheses.reasoning: Name similarity only; outside the province of Babylon as usually understood.

description: Plain in the province of Babylon where the image was set up (Dan 3:1). "Dura" may be a common noun ("walled place"). Location unknown; no coordinates are recorded.

hypotheses.label: Susa (Pleiades 912936)
hypotheses.reasoning: Pleiades representative point; capital of Elam and a Persian royal residence (Driver).

description: Capital of Elam and later a principal Persian royal residence (Neh 1:1; Esth 1:2).

hypotheses.label: Saimarreh/Eulaeus? (Pleiades 903109, uncertain)
hypotheses.reasoning: Pleiades marks the identification with a question mark; the point lies far upstream of Susa, whereas Daniel places the Ulai at Susa. The stream or canal at Susa is not precisely located in the sources read. The Saimarreh is the upper course of the Karkheh system, so this point and the Karkheh point refer to the same river system at different places.

hypotheses.label: Karkheh/Eulaeus? (Pleiades 912877, uncertain)
hypotheses.reasoning: Pleiades equates the Karkheh with the Eulaeus/Ulaya (with a "?"), and its point lies near Susa, where Daniel places the Ulai; T. G. Pinches (ISBE) judged "there is but little doubt" that the Ulai is the Kerkhah and notes the Assyrian Ulaia in Ashurbanipal's reliefs. Caveats: the river beds near Susa have shifted, and other candidates (the Shaur channel east of Susa, a canal, or the Karun/Coprates) are proposed in reference works not read in full. Kept below "certain".

description: River or canal at Susa where Daniel saw himself in the vision (8:2, 16). Exact course uncertain.

hypotheses.label: Tigris (Pleiades 912964, representative point)
hypotheses.reasoning: Hiddekel is the Tigris (Gen 2:14; Driver: Akkadian Idiglat). The point is Pleiades' representative point for the whole river; where on its banks Daniel stood is not stated.

description: River of Mesopotamia, Hebrew Hiddekel (Gen 2:14; Dan 10:4).

hypotheses.label: Riblah (Pleiades 431124909)
hypotheses.reasoning: Pleiades: town in Neo-Assyrian sources; modern Riblah about 35 km south of Homs, "in the land of Hamath" (2 Kgs 25:21).

description: Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters in Syria, where Zedekiah was judged (2 Kgs 25:6, 21).

hypotheses.label: Jericho (Pleiades 687917)
hypotheses.reasoning: Pleiades representative point; "the plains of Jericho" is the surrounding plain.

description: City in the Jordan valley; Zedekiah was overtaken in its plains (2 Kgs 25:5).

hypotheses.label: Tell en-Nasbeh (Pleiades 666067876)
hypotheses.reasoning: Pleiades attaches the name "Mizpah in Benjamin" to Tell en-Nasbeh with association certainty "less-certain"; recorded as probable, not certain.

description: Seat of Gedaliah's administration after 587/586 (2 Kgs 25:23; Jer 40:6).
Prophet from Tekoa (Amos 1:1).
King of Israel, son of Joash (Jehoash).
King of Judah; also called Azariah.
King of Babylon 605–562 BC.
King of Judah, son of Josiah; installed by Necho II.
Founder of the Neo-Babylonian dynasty; father of Nebuchadnezzar II.
Judean exile at the Babylonian and Persian courts; principal figure of the book of Daniel.
Pharaoh of Egypt.
Judean youth trained at the Babylonian court with Daniel.
Judean youth trained at the Babylonian court with Daniel. Distinct from other Hananiahs.
Judean youth trained at the Babylonian court with Daniel. Distinct from King Azariah (Uzziah) and other Azariahs.
Master of the eunuchs (chief court official) under Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 1:3).
Achaemenid king; conquered Babylon in 539 BC.
Captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard (Dan 2:14). Distinct from Arioch king of Ellasar (Gen 14:1).
Last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire (556–539 BC); spent about ten years at Tayma in Arabia.
Eldest son of Nabonidus (Bēl-šarra-uṣur), styled "son of the king" in Babylonian texts; exercised royal authority in Babylonia while Nabonidus was at Tayma. Called king in Daniel 5 and 7–8.
Governor of Gutium who entered Babylon with Cyrus's army "without a battle" on 16 Tašrītu and died on the night of 11 Arahsamna (ABC 7 iii 15–22). Often equated with the Gobryas of Xenophon.
Cyrus's official who appointed district officers in Babylon (ABC 7 iii 20). Whether he is the same man as Ugbaru is debated; the Livius translation spells them differently.

Ruler who "received the kingdom" after Belshazzar's death, aged about 62 (Dan 5:31); "son of Ahasuerus, of the offspring of the Medes" (Dan 9:1). Not named in any known contemporary source; identification disputed (see the Daniel 5 dossier).
Median king, son of Astyages and uncle of Cyrus, in Xenophon's Cyropaedia (1.5.2). Not attested in Herodotus or cuneiform sources; his historicity is debated.
Achaemenid king (522–486 BC), author of the Behistun inscription; organised the satrapies and their tribute (Herodotus 3.89). Distinct from "Darius the Mede" of Daniel 5–6.
Alexander III of Macedon (r. 336–323 BC), conqueror of the Persian empire.
Seleucid king (175–164 BC), son of Antiochus III and brother of Seleucus IV; formerly a hostage at Rome (1 Macc 1:10). Polybius records the nickname Epimanes, "madman".

Achaemenid king (accession 465/464, died 424/423 BC). The Artaxerxes of Ezra 7 and Nehemiah 2 is identified with him by most interpreters consulted; an identification of Ezra's Artaxerxes with Artaxerxes II is noted by Newton (Funccius) and is not adopted here.
Prophet of Judah from the 13th year of Josiah into the exile (Jer 1:1–3); his prophecy of seventy years (Jer 25:11–12; 29:10) is the subject of Daniel's prayer (Dan 9:2).

High priest at Jerusalem, supplanted by his brother Jason under Antiochus IV (2 Macc 4:7). 2 Maccabees has him killed near Antioch at Menelaus's instigation (4:33–35), c. 171 BC (Driver, after Schürer); Josephus's Jewish War (1.1.1) instead has "Onias the high priest" flee to Ptolemy and found the Heliopolis temple. Disputed (review open).

Achaemenid king (486–465 BC), son of Darius I; invaded Greece. Most interpreters read him as the rich fourth king of Dan 11:2; the "Ahasuerus" of Esther and Ezra 4:6 is usually identified with him (Driver).
Son of Lagus; satrap and then king of Egypt (d. 283/282 BC).
Founder of the Seleucid dynasty; once Ptolemy's officer, he became ruler of Babylon and Syria (d. 281 BC).
Seleucid king (261–246 BC) who married Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II.
Daughter of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, married to Antiochus II; killed with her son after his death (Jerome; Newton).
Second Ptolemaic king (283–246 BC); father of Berenice.
Third Ptolemaic king (246–222 BC); invaded the Seleucid realm to avenge his sister Berenice.
Seleucid king (246–225 BC), son of Antiochus II and Laodice.
Seleucid king (225–223 BC), elder son of Seleucus II; murdered on campaign.
Seleucid king (223–187 BC); defeated at Raphia (217), victorious at Panium (c. 200/198), defeated by Rome at Magnesia (190); killed in Elam (BM 35603).
Ptolemaic king (222–204 BC); victor at Raphia.
Ptolemaic king (204–180 BC), a child at accession; married Cleopatra I, daughter of Antiochus III.
Daughter of Antiochus III, married to Ptolemy V (betrothed in Antiochus's 7th year and married in his 13th, per Jerome); mother of Ptolemy VI.
Seleucid king, son of Antiochus III; reigned 12 years (BM 35603) and was assassinated in a conspiracy of Heliodorus (Appian, Syr. 45) in 175 BC.
Chancellor of Seleucus IV, sent for the Temple treasury in Jerusalem (2 Macc 3:7–28, with a miraculous repulse) and leader of the conspiracy in which the king was killed (Appian, Syr. 45).
Ptolemaic king (180–145 BC), son of Cleopatra I and nephew of Antiochus IV, whose invasions of Egypt (170–168) were ended by Roman intervention.
Roman envoy who in 168 BC ordered Antiochus IV out of Egypt, drawing a circle round him (Polybius 29.27). Jerome calls him "Marcus"; Driver and Polybius's editors "C(aius)".
Roman consul who defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC (Driver after Livy 37); Jerome mentions him with his brother Africanus.
Priest of Modein who began the revolt against Antiochus IV (1 Macc 2); Porphyry (per Jerome) took him as the "little help" of Dan 11:34.
Son of Mattathias; led the revolt and rededicated the Temple (1 Macc 3–4).

King of Judah for three months (598/597), son of Jehoiakim; surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in 597, held at Babylon, released by Amel-Marduk (Evil-merodach) in 561. Babylonian ration lists name him Ya'u-kīnu, king of Yahudu.
Last king of Judah (597–587/586), Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar (ABC 5: "a king of his own choice"); rebelled, captured and blinded at Riblah.
Babylonian "captain of the guard" who burned Jerusalem and deported its people (2 Kgs 25:8–20; Jer 52:12–30).
Appointed by Nebuchadnezzar over those left in Judah; governed from Mizpah and was assassinated by Ishmael son of Nethaniah in the seventh month (2 Kgs 25:22–25; Jer 40–41).
Member of the royal house who assassinated Gedaliah at Mizpah (2 Kgs 25:25; Jer 41).

King of Babylon, son of Nebuchadnezzar II; acceded October 562 and died August 560 BC (Parker & Dubberstein); released Jehoiachin in his accession year (2 Kgs 25:27). Josephus gives him eighteen years.
King of Judah for three months in 609 BC after Josiah's death; deposed by Necho II and taken to Egypt (2 Kgs 23:31–34; 2 Chr 36:1–4).

"Prince of Judah" who received the Temple vessels from Cyrus's treasurer and brought them to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:8–11); later said to have laid the Temple's foundation (Ezra 5:14–16). His relation to Zerubbabel is disputed.
Cyrus's treasurer who counted out the vessels to Sheshbazzar (Ezra 1:8). Distinct from the Mithredath of Ezra 4:7 under Artaxerxes.

title: The four kingdoms and the everlasting kingdom (Dan 2:36–45)
speaker: Daniel
description: Daniel's interpretation: Nebuchadnezzar is the head of gold; three further kingdoms follow, the fourth strong as iron and later divided; in the days of those kings God sets up an everlasting kingdom that breaks the others.
in_text_interpretation: Only the first kingdom is identified in the text (Nebuchadnezzar / Babylon). The second, third and fourth kingdoms and the stone are not named in Daniel 2.

interpretations.label: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome; the stone is the messianic kingdom
proponents: Josephus (iron as a world-ruling power; declines to explain the stone)
Talmud and medieval Jewish commentators incl. Rashi
interpretations.summary: The metals are a historical succession ending with Rome; God's kingdom (the Messiah's) replaces the world empires. Josephus already reads the bronze as a power "from the west" and the iron as a dominion over all the earth.

interpretations.label: Rome with a future ten-kingdom phase; the stone is Christ's return
interpretations.summary: The fourth kingdom is Rome; the ten toes correspond to a future revived Roman confederation (cf. 7:24; Rev 17:12), not yet realised; the stone is the Messiah, whose return decisively ends the world kingdoms.

interpretations.label: Rome followed by the divided nations of Europe; the stone is God's unending kingdom at Christ's return
interpretations.summary: A continuous fulfilment through history from Babylon to Rome and its divided successors, culminating in God's kingdom.

interpretations.label: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece (Seleucids and Ptolemies); the stone is God's imminent kingdom
proponents: S. R. Driver (1900): Introduction pp. x–xi ("in all probability the Median, Persian, and Greek"); Additional Note pp. 98–102 (this "Grecian" view first in Ephrem Syrus, then Ewald, Bleek, Delitzsch, Kuenen, Bevan)
Modern critical consensus, e.g. J. J. Collins (per Wikipedia)
Ephrem the Syrian; Polychronius; Cosmas Indicopleustes
interpretations.summary: Following Daniel's own sequence of Median and Persian rulers (5:31; 6:28), the four kingdoms are Babylon, Media, Persia and the Hellenistic kingdoms; the mixed iron and clay reflects Seleucid–Ptolemaic marriage alliances (c. 250 or 193 BC); the chapter in its present form dates from the early Seleucid period at the earliest. Driver (1900) holds this view and records that God's kingdom was expected to follow immediately on the fourth empire's overthrow in Antiochus Epiphanes (Introduction p. lxxxvii).

referents.referent: God's kingdom expected to replace Hellenistic rule

title: The decree of the watchers against the king (Dan 4:19–27)
speaker: Daniel
description: Daniel interprets the tree as the king, who will be driven from human society to live like an animal for seven times until he acknowledges the Most High, after which his kingdom is restored; he urges repentance.
in_text_interpretation: The text identifies the tree as Nebuchadnezzar and narrates its fulfilment within the chapter (4:28–33).

interpretations.label: Fulfilled in Nebuchadnezzar's seven-year madness
interpretations.summary: The decree was fulfilled in the king's own humbling for seven years (as the Old Greek renders it) and his restoration.

interpretations.label: Originally about Nabonidus
interpretations.summary: The tale is a variant of a tradition about Nabonidus's affliction and his long stay at Tayma (cf. 4Q242), transferred to the better-known Nebuchadnezzar. This is a source-critical view, not a fulfillment claim.

title: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN (Dan 5:24–28)
speaker: Daniel
description: Writing on the palace wall which Daniel reads as: God has numbered the kingdom and ended it; the king is weighed and found wanting; the kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.
in_text_interpretation: Daniel's reading (5:26–28) and the narrated sequel that night (5:30–31).

interpretations.label: Fulfilled that night in the fall of Babylon
interpretations.summary: The kingdom of Belshazzar ended when Babylon passed to Cyrus in October 539 BC.

referents.referent: Babylon given to the Medes and Persians

interpretations.label: Weights and wordplay
interpretations.summary: As nouns the words name weights — a mina, a shekel and half-pieces — which Daniel reinterprets as verbs; parsîn also puns on "Persia". If the half-pieces are two half-shekels the total is 62 shekels, the age given for Darius the Mede. This is a reading of the words, not a fulfillment claim.

title: The heavenly judgment and the kingdom given to the saints (Dan 7:9–12, 18, 21–22, 26–27)
speaker: Daniel (vision) and the attendant (interpretation)
description: The Ancient of Days holds court, the beast's dominion is taken away, and the kingdom is given to the people of the saints of the Most High forever.
in_text_interpretation: The judgment ends the horn's dominion (7:26) and gives the kingdom to the saints (7:22, 27). The Ancient of Days is not further identified.

interpretations.label: The Ancient of Days is God; a final judgment at the end of the age
proponents: D. Guzik (God the Father; kingdom on the millennial earth at Jesus' return)
interpretations.summary: Jerome reads the court as the last judgment and the kingdom as heavenly ("Away, then, with the fable about a millennium"); Guzik reads a future earthly kingdom received at Jesus' return. The two traditional readings disagree about the kingdom's nature.

interpretations.label: God's judgment on Antiochus and the expected kingdom of faithful Israel
interpretations.summary: The author expected God's kingdom to follow immediately on the fall of Antiochus (cf. 12:1–3); the expectation was not realised as described. Not a claim of fulfillment.

interpretations.label: The papal dominion taken away by degrees
interpretations.summary: After the 1260 years the dominion of the little horn is consumed "not at once, but by degrees", and the kingdom passes by degrees to the saints.

referents.referent: Gradual end of papal temporal power

interpretations.label: Later reuse: "Head of Days" in Enoch; the risen Christ with hair like wool (Rev 1:14)
interpretations.summary: Enoch renames the Ancient of Days the "Head of Days"; Revelation transfers the white wool and snow of the Ancient of Days to the "one like a son of man". Recorded as reception, not as a fulfillment.

referents.referent: Head of Days (Enoch); features applied to Christ (Rev 1:14)

title: One like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion (Dan 7:13–14)
speaker: Daniel (vision report)
description: A human-like figure comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom that all peoples will serve and that will never be destroyed.
in_text_interpretation: The figure is not explicitly identified. In the interpretation the everlasting kingdom is given to "the saints of the Most High" / "the people of the saints of the Most High" (7:18, 22, 27).

interpretations.label: Jesus as the Son of Man (Christian messianic)
proponents: Gospel tradition: Jesus' reply at his trial (Mark 14:62; Matt 26:64)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: Jesus' self-designation "the Son of Man … coming with the clouds" (Mark 14:62) cites Dan 7:13; Revelation 1:13 describes the risen Christ as "one like a son of man". Objections (Driver): the chapter's own interpretation applies the kingdom to the saints, not to an individual. Acceptance: Montgomery calls the personal messianic view the eldest and formerly prevailing one; the historicity of individual Gospel sayings was not researched here.

referents.symbol: One like a son of man

interpretations.label: An individual Messiah (Second Temple and rabbinic Jewish)
proponents: b. Sanhedrin 98a (R. Alexandri for R. Joshua b. Levi)
interpretations.summary: Enoch's Son of Man stands beside the "Head of Days" and judges kings; 2 Esdras 13 has a man rising from the sea and flying with the clouds; the Talmud reads Dan 7:13 as the Messiah's coming if Israel is worthy, and Akiva read the thrones as one for God and one for David (disputed by R. Yose). Not a claim of historical fulfillment.

referents.symbol: One like a son of man

interpretations.label: A symbol of the people of the saints (collective)
interpretations.summary: As the beasts stand for kingdoms, the human figure stands for the ideal Israel to whom 7:18, 22 and 27 give the same everlasting kingdom; human form contrasts with bestial empires, the clouds mark God's action. Montgomery calls this "itself an ancient view". Objection: the figure is distinguished from the saints and approaches God like an individual (traditional readers).

referents.symbol: One like a son of man
referents.referent: The people of the saints of the Most High (ideal Israel)

interpretations.label: An angelic leader (Michael)
proponents: J. J. Collins (1998, pp. 101–103), via Wikipedia — not read directly
interpretations.summary: The figure is the angelic prince of Israel (cf. Michael in 10:13, 21; 12:1), and "the holy ones" may be angels. Wikipedia calls this "the main alternative view"; known here only at second hand.

referents.symbol: One like a son of man
referents.referent: Michael, the angelic leader of God's host

title: The ten horns and the little horn: time, times and half a time (Dan 7:8, 20–26)
speaker: An attendant in the vision
description: Ten kings arise from the fourth kingdom; another king subdues three, blasphemes, persecutes the saints and attempts to change times and law for a time, times and half a time, until the judgment removes his dominion.
in_text_interpretation: Horns = kings (7:24). The duration is "a time and times and half a time" (7:25). No king is named.

interpretations.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the Seleucid kings
interpretations.summary: The ten horns are Seleucid kings (several reconstructions; the three uprooted are e.g. Heliodorus, Demetrius and Ptolemy VI, or alternatives); the little horn is Antiochus IV, whose suppression of Temple worship (1 Macc 1:41–64) lasted about three and a half years. Objections: the identity and number of the ten and the three are uncertain (Driver concedes "our knowledge … does not … enable us to decide"); Jerome objects that Porphyry's three kings do not fit; conservative readers object that the everlasting kingdom did not follow Antiochus's death.

referents.symbol: Time, times and half a time

interpretations.label: A future Antichrist from a ten-fold division of the Roman world
interpretations.summary: At the end of the age ten kings partition the Roman world; an eleventh overthrows three and persecutes the saints for three and a half literal years before Christ's return (Jerome; Guzik links Rev 11–13). Objection (Driver): the kingdoms must arise from the fourth empire, which no longer exists. Not a claim of historical fulfillment.

referents.symbol: Time, times and half a time

interpretations.label: The papacy (historicist)
interpretations.summary: The ten horns are the kingdoms into which the Western Empire broke; the little horn is the Church of Rome as a temporal power, which subdued three of them; "time, times and half a time" is 1260 years on a day-for-a-year reckoning (Newton). Objection (Driver): the scheme is "non-natural" and depends on choosing ten kingdoms and a starting date.

referents.referent: Kingdoms of the Western Roman Empire

referents.symbol: Time, times and half a time

interpretations.label: Julius Caesar and the Caesars
proponents: J. Calvin (as reported by Guzik; not read directly)
interpretations.summary: The little horn is the line of Roman Caesars beginning with Julius Caesar. Recorded as reported by Enduring Word, which rejects it.

title: The four kingdoms and the kingdom of the saints (Dan 7:17–18, 23, 27)
speaker: An attendant in the vision
description: Four beasts are four kings/kingdoms; the fourth differs from the rest; afterwards the saints of the Most High receive an everlasting kingdom.
in_text_interpretation: Four kings (7:17); the fourth beast a fourth kingdom (7:23). The text names none of the kingdoms; Daniel 2:38 identifies the first kingdom of the parallel dream with Nebuchadnezzar.

interpretations.label: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome ("Roman" scheme)
interpretations.framework: Traditional Christian (patristic); also later Jewish authorities
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the parallel with the four-metal statue of ch. 2; Medes and Persians as one kingdom (cf. 8:20); Rome as the iron power that crushed all. Objection (Driver 1900): no ten kingdoms arise out of Rome, which has passed away, and the little horn of ch. 7 matches the Antiochus horn of ch. 8. Acceptance: general among the Church Fathers (Driver); held today mainly in conservative interpretation (not quantified in sources read).

interpretations.label: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece ("Grecian" scheme)
proponents: Ewald, Bleek, Delitzsch, Kuenen, Bevan (via Driver)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: Daniel presents a separate Median kingdom (Darius the Mede, 5:31; 9:1) before Persia; the little horn here matches that of ch. 8 (Antiochus), whose persecution lasts the same "time, times and half a time" (cf. 12:7); the book's horizon ends with Antiochus. Objection: no independent Median empire ruled Babylon between Nabonidus and Cyrus (ABC 7); the bear/three ribs fit Medo-Persia (Driver concedes as plausible). Acceptance: the standard critical reading (Driver 1900; Levine via Wikipedia); a precise modern percentage was not found.

interpretations.label: Porphyry: the leopard is Alexander, the fourth beast his successors
interpretations.framework: Anti-Christian philosophical critique (3rd century AD), known through Jerome
interpretations.summary: Porphyry merged the Macedonian and Roman beasts into one Macedonian realm, made the fourth beast the successors of Alexander and counted ten cruel kings up to Antiochus Epiphanes. Jerome rejected this. Porphyry's own work survives only in such quotations.

referents.referent: Ten kings up to Antiochus IV

title: The ram, the goat and the four kingdoms (Dan 8:3–8, 20–22)
speaker: Gabriel
description: The kings of Media and Persia are overthrown by the king of Greece, whose first king is broken and replaced by four kingdoms of lesser power.
in_text_interpretation: Explicit: ram = the kings of Media and Persia; goat = the king of Greece; great horn = the first king; four horns = four kingdoms from his nation (8:20–22).

interpretations.label: Alexander the Great and his successors
interpretations.framework: Common to traditional and critical interpreters
proponents: Josephus (Ant. 11.8.5, Alexander told he was meant)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the text itself names Media, Persia and Greece; Alexander, the first Macedonian king of Asia, defeated Darius III (Arbela, 331 BC) and died young; his empire passed to successors. Objections/variants: the four are listed differently — Jerome: Ptolemy, Philip Arrhidaeus, Seleucus, Antigonus; Guzik: Cassander, Lysimachus, Seleucus, Ptolemy (the coalition against Antigonus, Diodorus 20.106). Acceptance: no dissent found among the sources consulted on the identification of the great horn with Alexander.

referents.referent: The kingdoms of Alexander's successors (lists differ)

title: The little horn and the king of fierce face (Dan 8:9–12, 23–25)
speaker: Gabriel
description: From one of the four kingdoms a fierce, cunning king arises who destroys the holy people, removes the continual offering, opposes the prince of princes, and is broken without human hand.
in_text_interpretation: The little horn is a king arising "in the latter time of their kingdom" (8:23) — i.e. of the four kingdoms of Greece. He is not named.

interpretations.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
proponents: Josephus (Ant. 12.7.6: the desolation "according to the prophecy of Daniel")
S. R. Driver (1900): "admitted on all hands"
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the horn comes from one of the four Greek kingdoms; it removes the continual offering and desolates the sanctuary, which 1 Maccabees records under Antiochus (1:54) until the rededication (4:52). Objection (Newton): a horn signifies a kingdom, not one man, and Antiochus's kingdom was not "exceedingly great". Acceptance: Driver says it is "admitted on all hands"; even Jerome, who resists Antiochus for ch. 7, accepts him here.

referents.symbol: Little horn / king of fierce face

interpretations.label: Antiochus as a type of the future Antichrist (dual fulfillment)
interpretations.summary: Because the vision concerns "the time of the end" (8:17, 19), the near fulfillment in Antiochus prefigures a final Antichrist. The future part is not a claim of historical fulfillment; the Antiochus part is recorded separately.

referents.referent: Antiochus as type; the Antichrist as antitype

interpretations.label: Rome (historicist)
interpretations.summary: The little horn of the goat is a new kingdom that arose out of one of the four — Rome, which conquered Macedonia and the East and later continued as the Greek empire. Newton rejects Antiochus "not very judiciously" identified. Objection (Driver): the horn grows "out of one of them", i.e. from a Greek kingdom, and its deeds match Antiochus's.

title: 2,300 evenings and mornings until the sanctuary is cleansed (Dan 8:13–14, 26)
speaker: A holy one
description: The desolation of the sanctuary and suspension of the continual offering will last 2,300 evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be cleansed.
in_text_interpretation: The text gives the number and says the vision is "true" and for "many days to come" (8:26); it does not say whether the unit is a day or a single offering.

interpretations.label: 1,150 days (2,300 offerings) of the interrupted sacrifice under Antiochus
interpretations.summary: The continual offering was made morning and evening, so 2,300 offerings = 1,150 days, a little under the 3 years 10 days between the desecration (15 Chislev 145) and the rededication (25 Chislev 148). Objection (Driver himself): the figure does "not agree precisely with the event".

interpretations.label: 2,300 days ending with the cleansing of the Temple
proponents: Jerome (six years and three months from year 143)
D. Guzik (from 171 BC, Menelaus's high priesthood, to the cleansing)
interpretations.summary: Evening-morning = a full day (cf. Gen 1:5), so 2,300 days ≈ 6⅓ years ending with Judas Maccabaeus's rededication. The starting point differs between proponents; Driver lists further variants (e.g. Dec 168 to the defeat of Nicanor, 161).

interpretations.label: 2,300 years from 457 BC to AD 1843 (year-day)
interpretations.summary: A prophetic day equals a year; the period begins with Artaxerxes' decree to Ezra (457 BC, the start of the seventy weeks of Dan 9) and ends in AD 1843 with the cleansing of the sanctuary at Christ's return. Objection (Guzik): Daniel's vision concerns Antiochus and the Temple cleansing commemorated in John 10:22; Miller's reckoning is rejected. Later Adventist reinterpretations (1844) were not researched from primary sources.

title: Jeremiah's seventy years (Jer 25:11–12; 29:10; read in Dan 9:2)
speaker: Jeremiah
description: The nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years; when they are completed Babylon will be punished (Jer 25:11–12) and the exiles visited and returned (29:10). Daniel reads it as seventy years "for the desolations of Jerusalem" (Dan 9:2).
in_text_interpretation: Later biblical texts apply it differently: 2 Chr 36:21–22 to the land's sabbath rest until the kingdom of Persia and Cyrus's first year; Zech 1:12 (Darius's second year) to "these seventy years" of indignation against Jerusalem; Dan 9:24 extends it to seventy weeks.

interpretations.label: Babylonian supremacy: c. 609/605 to 539/538 BC
proponents: S. R. Driver (1900): "the 70 years of the Chaldaean supremacy"
D. Guzik (counting from 605, the first deportation)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: Jer 25:11 speaks of the nations serving the king of Babylon; 25:12 ends the period with Babylon's punishment. Historical evidence: Babylon fell in Oct 539 (Nabonidus Chronicle) and Cyrus's first Babylonian year began Nisan 538. Objection: 605–539 is 66 years, so "seventy" is taken as round or the end point moved later (Guzik: the period still had "three or four years" to run at Dan 9).

referents.referent: From Babylon's rise over Judah to its fall

interpretations.label: Desolation of the Temple: 587/586 to 516/515 BC
proponents: Zechariah 1:12; 7:5 (text, in Darius I's 2nd and 4th years)
Jerome ("seventy years for the desolation of the Temple")
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: in Darius I's second year (Zech 1:7, 12) the angel still speaks of "these seventy years" of indignation against Jerusalem, and the Temple was finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15). From the destruction (587/586) to the completion (Adar 515) is about 70 years (operator arithmetic). Objection: Jeremiah's own wording is about serving Babylon, not the Temple.

referents.referent: From the Temple's destruction to its rebuilding

interpretations.label: The land's sabbaths, ended by Cyrus's decree (Chronicler)
interpretations.summary: The Chronicler joins Jeremiah's seventy years to the land enjoying its sabbaths (Lev 26:34–35) "until the reign of the kingdom of Persia", and dates Cyrus's proclamation to his first year "that the LORD's word by Jeremiah's mouth might be accomplished". Driver notes that Dan 9:24 develops this sabbatical reading into seventy weeks of years. Guzik: about 490 years of neglected sabbath years left the land owing seventy, collected in the exile; he gives no start or end year.

referents.referent: The land's sabbath rest until Cyrus

title: The seventy weeks (Dan 9:24–27)
speaker: Gabriel
description: Seventy weeks are decreed on Daniel's people and city: seven weeks from a word to rebuild Jerusalem to an anointed prince; sixty-two weeks of rebuilding in troubled times; then an anointed one is cut off, a coming prince's people destroy city and sanctuary, a covenant is made for one week, and in its middle sacrifice ceases and an abomination makes desolate. Jerome already found the passage argued "in various ways by men of greatest learning"; Driver calls it the most discussed passage of the Old Testament. Origen (as reported by Jerome) only urged that the years from Darius's first year to Christ be ascertained.
in_text_interpretation: The text gives the divisions 7 + 62 + 1 (= 70) weeks and the events attached to them. It does not define a "week", name the decree, the anointed one(s), the prince who comes, or the subject of "he will make a firm covenant", and gives no calendar.

interpretations.label: Maccabean: 587 BC to Cyrus, to the murder of Onias III (171), to Antiochus IV (164)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the "word" is Jeremiah's promise of rebuilding (Jer 30–31, c. 587); seven weeks (49 years) bring "an anointed one, a prince" — Cyrus (Isa 45:1), 538 (Graetz and Bevan: Jeshua); the "anointed one cut off" after 62 more weeks is the high priest Onias III (2 Macc 4:33–35, c. 171); the coming prince is Antiochus IV, whose suspension of sacrifice for half a week matches 167–164. Historical evidence: 1–2 Maccabees. Objections: 538 to 171 is 367 years, not 434 — "too large by 67" (Driver); defenders explain it as a mistaken chronology, citing similar over-estimates by Demetrius and Josephus (Schürer). Acceptance: Driver adopts it as the principal alternative to the traditional view; Montgomery says no period "so neatly fits".

referents.symbol: Prince who comes; he who causes sacrifice to cease

interpretations.label: Maccabean variant: overlapping weeks from Jer 25 (605 BC)
proponents: G. Behrmann (both as reported by Driver)
interpretations.summary: The word is Jer 25 (606/605); the seven weeks end c. 558 while the 62 weeks run concurrently from the same point to 171; the last week ends 164. Objection (Driver): Jer 25 contains a rebuilding promise only implicitly, and the text gives no hint that the 62 weeks do not follow the 7.

interpretations.label: Messianic, continuous: from Artaxerxes' seventh year (Ezra 7) to Christ
proponents: Auberlen and Pusey (as reported by Driver)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: 490 years run from Ezra's commission (Artaxerxes I year 7; Newton: Julian Period 4257, 458/457 BC) to Christ's death, which "made reconciliation"; Newton counts the 62 weeks separately from Nehemiah's wall (28th year? — Newton) to Christ's birth and applies the seven weeks to the second coming; Miller counts 457 BC + 490 = AD 33. Objections (Driver): Ezra 7 says nothing of rebuilding Jerusalem; the RV punctuation separates the 7 and 62 weeks; Christ's ministry lasted about 3½ years, not a week; the destruction of AD 70 falls outside the 490 years.

referents.symbol: People of the prince who comes

interpretations.label: Messianic with a gap: 69 weeks from Artaxerxes' twentieth year to the triumphal entry; the 70th week future
proponents: Sir Robert Anderson, The Coming Prince (1881)
D. Guzik (also citing Walvoord and Ironside)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: only Neh 2 commands the city and wall to be built; 69 weeks of 360-day "prophetic years" (173,880 days) run from 1 Nisan of Artaxerxes' 20th year, which Anderson fixes at 14 March 445 BC from an astronomical new moon supplied by the Astronomer Royal, to 6 April AD 32, Jesus' entry into Jerusalem; after the 69th week comes "a gap or parenthesis" and the 70th week is future, with the coming prince as Antichrist. Objections: Guzik himself notes AD 32 is controversial (most chronologists prefer AD 30 or 33); Driver insists the weeks run consecutively and have the same value; Parker & Dubberstein's Babylonian table puts 1 Nisan of Artaxerxes' 20th year on 13 April, not 14 March, 445 (operator comparison — the Judean calendar may have differed). Acceptance: widely held in dispensational circles (not quantified in sources read). Arithmetic (operator check): in Julian reckoning the stated dates are 173,882 days apart; Anderson's 173,880 applies a Gregorian leap-year correction to Julian dates (his own note).

referents.symbol: He who makes a firm covenant

interpretations.label: Africanus: Artaxerxes' 20th year to Christ in lunar years (reported by Jerome)
proponents: Julius Africanus, Chronographiae book 5 (quoted by Jerome)
interpretations.summary: Counts from Artaxerxes' 20th year (Ol. 83.4) to the 15th year of Tiberius (Ol. 202.2): 475 solar years, which, reckoned in Hebrew lunar years with intercalation, make 490. Reckoning from Cyrus or from Daniel's vision falls short; from the start of the captivity it overshoots.

referents.referent: From Nehemiah's commission to Christ's passion

interpretations.label: Eusebius (1): the anointed are the high priests from Jeshua to Alexander Jannaeus (reported by Jerome)
interpretations.summary: From Cyrus, 7 weeks cover the long-delayed rebuilding of the Temple; 62 weeks (483 years in all) run through the succession of anointed high priests to the death of Alexander Jannaeus, after which civil strife, Pompey and Herod ended the legitimate line.

interpretations.label: Eusebius (2): from Darius's sixth year to Herod; the half-week is Christ's ministry (reported by Jerome)
proponents: Eusebius of Caesarea (Chronicle; reported by Jerome)
interpretations.summary: 69 weeks run from the completion of the Temple in Darius's sixth year to Herod's seizure of Judaea and the murder of Hyrcanus; Christ preached 3½ years and after his passion sacrifice ceased "in the middle of the week". Eusebius also reports a view that the last week was seventy years (Nero to Trajan), which Jerome finds inconsistent.

interpretations.label: Hippolytus: 62 weeks to Christ's birth; the last week at the end of the world (reported by Jerome)
interpretations.summary: Seven weeks precede the return from Babylon, sixty-two run to Christ's birth, and the final week is divided between Elijah and the Antichrist at the end of the age. Jerome objects that the Persian and Macedonian periods give about 560 years, not 483.

referents.referent: Elijah and the Antichrist at the end of the world

interpretations.label: Apollinaris of Laodicea: from Christ's birth; a future rebuilding and Antichrist (reported by Jerome)
interpretations.summary: Counts from the "going forth of the Word" at Christ's birth: 7 weeks to the eighth year of Claudius, then 62 weeks (434 years), after which Jerusalem would be rebuilt in the last week, Elijah would come and the Antichrist sit in the Temple. Jerome warns that later generations would have to convict him of error if the dates failed; no historical fulfillment is claimed here.

referents.referent: Christ's birth to a future end

interpretations.label: Clement of Alexandria: Cyrus to Vespasian and Titus (reported by Jerome)
interpretations.summary: The seventy weeks span the Persian, Macedonian and Roman ages from Cyrus to the destruction of the Temple under Vespasian and Titus. Jerome objects that this interval is about 630 years.

interpretations.label: Tertullian: from Darius's first year to Christ's birth (62½ weeks) and to Vespasian (70 weeks) (reported by Jerome)
proponents: Tertullian, Against the Jews (quoted by Jerome)
interpretations.summary: Begins at the first year of Darius, when the vision was given; Persian, Macedonian and Ptolemaic reigns total 437½ years to Christ's birth in Augustus's 41st year; adding the emperors to Vespasian's capture of Jerusalem completes the seventy weeks. The regnal figures are Tertullian's own and do not match modern chronology.

interpretations.label: "The Hebrews": from Darius the Mede to the destructions under Vespasian and Hadrian (reported by Jerome)
interpretations.framework: Jewish interpretation of Jerome's day (as reported by a Christian author)
interpretations.summary: From the first year of Darius (who slew Belshazzar), the city and Temple are rebuilt; the 62 weeks run to the perpetual desolation under Vespasian, and the single week is split between Vespasian (3½ years of peace) and Hadrian's final war. Jerome objects that the interval is 696 years. This is a hostile witness's paraphrase; rabbinic sources were not read directly.

referents.symbol: People of the prince who comes

interpretations.label: Symbolic weeks: from Cyrus's word to Christ, the age of the church, and the last enemy
interpretations.framework: Symbolic (non-chronological) reading; conservative Lutheran, amillennial-type (Keil after Kliefoth and Leyrer)
proponents: Th. Kliefoth and Leyrer (as followed by Keil)
J. Baldwin ("symbolic and not arithmetical", as quoted by Guzik)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: šābûaʿ means "a period of sevens" without fixing the unit, while Daniel elsewhere uses exact measures (8:14 evenings-mornings; 12:11 days); the answer to Daniel's question about seventy years is a divine measure, not a calendar. The seven sevens run from the word to rebuild (Isa 44:28, Cyrus) to the Messiah; the sixty-two are the building of God's city in troubled times; the last seven is the final enemy's rule and judgment. Every chronological reckoning, Keil argues, does violence to the text or fails arithmetically; the times of the end are reserved to God (Acts 1:7; Mark 13:32). Objections: Guzik criticises commentators who ignore the numbers; Driver requires weeks of equal value in order; preterist and dispensational readers both treat the numbers as calendrical.

referents.referent: From Cyrus's word to the coming of Christ
The age of the Messiah's kingdom in troubled times
The final enemy and the consummation

title: The princes of Persia and Greece and Michael (Dan 10:13, 20–21)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: A heavenly conflict: the prince of Persia resists, Michael helps, and the prince of Greece "will come". The chapter introduces the revelation of 11:2–12:4.
in_text_interpretation: Michael is "your prince" — the prince of Daniel's people (10:21; 12:1). The princes of Persia and Greece are not otherwise identified.

interpretations.label: Patron (guardian) angels of the nations
proponents: Jerome (citing Deut 32:8: "according to the number of the angels of God")
interpretations.summary: Each nation has an angelic prince in heaven whose success matches its own; Michael is Israel's. Textual reasoning: Deut 32:8 in the LXX (and a reading Driver notes some think original) divides the nations "according to the number of the sons/angels of God"; Sir 17:17; Isa 24:21. Driver: the doctrine of tutelary angels appears distinctly for the first time here, developed later into seventy angel-princes of the nations (Targum Ps.-Jonathan, as cited by Driver). This is a statement about the text's worldview, not a historical claim.

interpretations.label: Hostile spiritual powers (high-ranking demons) opposing God's purposes
proponents: D. Guzik (citing Walvoord, Wood and Baldwin)
interpretations.summary: The prince of Persia is "a demon of high rank", not a human ruler; prayer is linked to unseen conflict (cf. Eph 6:12; John 12:31). Guzik rejects reading the prince as a human king.

interpretations.label: The coming of the prince of Greece = the Macedonian overthrow of Persia
interpretations.summary: After the Jews were freed, Alexander slew Darius and overthrew the Persians and Medes, so that "the prince of the Greeks did overcome the prince of the Persians". Historical evidence: Arrian on Gaugamela (331) and Darius III's death (330). Objection: the text speaks of heavenly princes, and the link to a particular event is the interpreter's.

referents.referent: The rise of Alexander's Macedon against Persia

title: The king who exalts himself (Dan 11:36–45)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: The king does according to his will, magnifies himself above every god, honours a god of fortresses; at the time of the end he overruns the glorious land and Egypt, is troubled by news from east and north, plants his tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain, and comes to his end with no one to help.
in_text_interpretation: No name or date; "at the time of the end" (11:40).

interpretations.label: Antiochus IV continued; 11:40–45 an unfulfilled or idealised forecast of his end
proponents: Porphyry (per Jerome, with a fourth Egyptian campaign)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: "the king" continues the subject of 11:21–35; Antiochus's divine titles and Hellenising religious policy fit 11:36–39. But 11:40–45 (a final conquest of Egypt, death between the sea and the holy mountain) does not match the record: Antiochus went east in 166/165 and died at Tabae in Persia (Polybius 31.9; BM 35603, 164 BC). Driver: the prophecy correctly foretold his speedy doom, while the circumstances "do not correspond to what we know of the historical reality" — like details in earlier prophets. Porphyry's fourth Egyptian expedition is known only through Jerome and conflicts with Roman protection of Egypt (Bevan, via Driver).

referents.symbol: He will come to his end

interpretations.label: A future Antichrist (transition at 11:36)
proponents: D. Guzik (Antiochus a "trailer", the Antichrist the "feature")
interpretations.summary: The king of 11:36–45 is the end-time Antichrist who sits in the Temple as God (2 Thess 2:4); he dies between the seas at the holy mountain (Jerome: near the Mount of Olives, with Apedno = "his throne"). Guzik places the transition at 11:36 and speculates that the king of the north may be Russia. Future reference; not a claim of historical fulfilment. Objection (Driver): there is no break in the text at 11:36.

interpretations.label: The Byzantine "Greek" empire; king of the south = Saracens, king of the north = Turks (historicist)
interpretations.summary: After the division of the Roman empire, "the king" is the empire of the Greeks, which honoured "Mahuzzims" (the saints and their relics) and forbade marriage to monks; at the time of the end the Saracens (south) and Turks (north) attacked it, and the Turkish empire took Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia. Objection: requires the subject to change several times without textual signal.

title: The kings of the south and the north (Dan 11:5–20)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: A sequence of wars and marriage alliances between the king of the south and the king of the north, ending with a raiser of taxes who is destroyed "not in anger, and not in battle".
in_text_interpretation: The text calls them only "the king of the south" and "the king of the north"; it names Egypt (11:8) and "the glorious land" (11:16) and no persons.

interpretations.label: Ptolemies and Seleucids from Ptolemy I to Seleucus IV
interpretations.framework: Agreed by Porphyry and Jerome; followed by historicist, critical and evangelical commentators
proponents: Porphyry (per Jerome: "no point of controversy" up to 11:20)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the sequence matches the Ptolemaic (south) and Seleucid (north) kings as seen from Judaea. 11:5 Ptolemy I and his former officer Seleucus I; 11:6 Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, married to Antiochus II and killed after his death; 11:7–9 her brother Ptolemy III invades and carries off gods and treasure; 11:10 the sons of Seleucus II — Seleucus III and Antiochus III; 11:11–12 Ptolemy IV wins at Raphia (Polybius 5.82–87) but does not follow up; 11:13–16 Antiochus III returns, defeats Scopas at Panium and takes Judaea (Polybius 16.18–19, 39); 11:17 Cleopatra I given to Ptolemy V; 11:18 Antiochus turns to the coastlands and is stopped by a Roman commander (Lucius Scipio, Magnesia); 11:19 he dies in his own land (BM 35603: "killed in Elam"); 11:20 Seleucus IV, whose minister Heliodorus was sent for the Temple money, killed by conspiracy (Appian, Syr. 45). Historical evidence: Polybius, Appian, the Babylonian king list. Objection: the correlations are made by the interpreters; Daniel names no one.

referents.symbol: Daughter of the king of the south

interpretations.label: Variants at 11:20: Ptolemy V (Porphyry), Trypho ("the Hebrews"), Seleucus III (Guzik)
interpretations.framework: Minority variants reported by Jerome; Guzik
interpretations.summary: Porphyry took the raiser of taxes to be Ptolemy V Epiphanes; "the Hebrews" took the vile one of 11:20–21 to be Trypho; Guzik names "Seleucus III, the eldest son of Antiochus III". Objections: Jerome answers that Ptolemy did not rise "in the place" of Antiochus III; the Babylonian king list makes Seleucus IV (not Seleucus III, who preceded Antiochus III) the son who succeeded Antiochus III and reigned 12 years.

interpretations.label: 11:14: the Onias temple at Leontopolis (Jerome)
interpretations.summary: "The children of the violent among your people … to establish the vision" are the Jews who followed the high priest Onias to Egypt and built a rival temple (citing Isa 19:19); Driver instead refers the verse to Jews who sided with Antiochus III (not read in full). The dating of the Leontopolis temple (later than Antiochus III) is a problem for Jerome's reading.

title: Four kings of Persia; the fourth stirs up all against Greece (Dan 11:2)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: Three more kings will arise in Persia; the fourth, far richer, will stir up all against the realm of Greece.
in_text_interpretation: The text names Persia and Greece (Yavan) but no king.

interpretations.label: Cambyses, (Pseudo-)Smerdis, Darius I, Xerxes
proponents: S. R. Driver (counting Gaumata, or with Cyrus included)
interpretations.summary: After Cyrus (10:1) come Cambyses, the Magian Smerdis/Gaumata and Darius I; the fourth is Xerxes, whose wealth and invasion of Greece match the verse (Herodotus 7). Driver prefers counting Cyrus as the first, so that Gaumata may be omitted and Xerxes is still the fourth. Jerome rejects identifying the fourth with Darius III, who was "the fourteenth" king after Cyrus.

interpretations.label: Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius I; Xerxes the fourth
proponents: D. Guzik (the count may omit Cyrus or Smerdis)
interpretations.summary: Newton counts Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius Hystaspes as the three and Xerxes as the fourth. Guzik names only Xerxes and leaves the count open. Objection (all readings): Daniel then passes over the remaining Persian kings to Alexander — Jerome: Scripture "summarizes only the most important matters".

title: A mighty king and the fourfold division of his kingdom (Dan 11:3–4)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: A mighty king rules with great dominion; at his height his kingdom is broken toward the four winds, not to his posterity.
in_text_interpretation: The text does not name the king; it parallels the goat's great horn (8:8, 21–22), which the text calls "the first king" of Greece.

interpretations.label: Alexander the Great and the partition among his generals
interpretations.framework: Common to patristic, historicist, critical and evangelical interpreters
interpretations.summary: Alexander died young and his heirs did not inherit; the empire was divided among his generals (Jerome: Ptolemy, Philip Arrhidaeus, Seleucus, Antigonus; Newton: Ptolemy, Antigonus, Lysimachus, Cassander, with Seleucus later). "Others besides these" (11:4) = lesser kingdoms (Jerome). Acceptance: no dissent found among sources consulted.

title: The contemptible person (Dan 11:21–35)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: A contemptible person takes the kingdom by flattery, breaks the prince of the covenant, invades the south twice, is turned back by ships of Kittim, profanes the sanctuary, removes the continual offering and sets up the abomination that makes desolate; the wise suffer and receive "a little help".
in_text_interpretation: The text gives no name. "Kittim" (11:30) is a place-name (Cyprus/western coastlands, Driver); "the abomination that makes desolate" recurs in 9:27 and 12:11.

interpretations.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes, 175–167 BC
interpretations.framework: Porphyry; historical-critical; also the near fulfilment in evangelical readings
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the contemptible person replaces the raiser of taxes (Seleucus IV) without hereditary right (Antiochus IV replaced his brother's son); "the prince of the covenant" broken = Onias III deposed in 175 (Driver) or the young Ptolemy VI; two Egyptian campaigns (170–169, 168); "ships of Kittim" = the Roman envoys and Popillius Laenas at Eleusis (Polybius 29.27); the Temple plundered (1 Macc 1:20–24) and the abomination set up on 15 Chislev 145 (1 Macc 1:54); "a little help" = Mattathias and the Maccabees (Porphyry). Historical evidence: Polybius, Appian, 1–2 Maccabees, BM 35603. Acceptance: Jerome concedes "there is no doubt" Antiochus did several of these things while reading them as typological.

referents.referent: The pagan altar of 15 Chislev 145 SE

interpretations.label: The Antichrist, with Antiochus as a type
proponents: Jerome and the Christian writers he follows
interpretations.summary: From 11:21 the prophecy speaks of the Antichrist at the end of the world; Antiochus's deeds are preliminary "types" (as Solomon prefigures Christ in Ps 72). Jerome nevertheless reports the Antiochus history verse by verse. Future reference; not a claim of historical fulfilment.

interpretations.label: Jewish readings reported by Jerome: the Romans (11:31) and Julian (11:34)
interpretations.framework: Jewish interpretation of Jerome's day (hostile report)
interpretations.summary: The ships of Kittim are the Romans; Vespasian's son Titus profaned the sanctuary and removed the continual sacrifice; the "little help" was the emperor Julian (or Severus and Antoninus), who favoured the Jews. Known only through Jerome.

interpretations.label: From 11:31 the Romans; the little help is Constantine (historicist)
interpretations.summary: After the Roman conquest of Macedon, "arms" = the Romans, who polluted the sanctuary and placed the abomination (Hadrian's temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, AD 132; Matt 24:15 puts it after Christ); the persecuted Christians were helped "with a little help" by Constantine. Objection: Driver and Porphyry read 11:31 as continuing the same king's actions.

title: Michael, the time of trouble and the resurrection (Dan 12:1–3)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: Michael stands up for Daniel's people in an unequalled time of trouble; those written in the book are delivered; many who sleep in the dust awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt; the wise shine like the stars.
in_text_interpretation: The text says "many" (not "all") will awake, in two groups; it names Michael "the great prince who stands for the children of your people" and gives no date beyond "at that time".

interpretations.label: Bodily resurrection of the dead at the end; two resurrections
proponents: D. Guzik (citing Baldwin: "many" can mean all)
interpretations.summary: After the Antichrist is destroyed, the dead rise, some to life and some to shame (Jerome); Guzik adds that the resurrections to life and to condemnation are separated in time (John 5:29; Rev 20:4–6) and that the time of trouble is the Great Tribulation (Jer 30:7; Matt 24:21). Jerome argues the trouble cannot be Antiochus's, since the Babylonian destruction was worse. Future reference; not a claim of historical fulfilment.

referents.referent: The Great Tribulation / the Antichrist's persecution

interpretations.label: A resurrection of prominent Israelites (martyrs and apostates) expected after Antiochus's fall
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the first Old Testament passage to teach a resurrection of the wicked as well as the righteous and differing destinies (cf. Isa 26:19, limited to Israel); "many" = those who had conspicuously helped or hindered God's kingdom under Antiochus. Driver: the writer expected the kingdom to follow the tyrant's fall, which it did not — like earlier prophets whose ideal hopes were not realised at once. Later developments: 1 Enoch, 2 Macc 7, the Targums. No historical fulfilment is claimed. The same hope appears in the martyr narrative of 2 Macc 7 ("the King of the world will raise us … up", 7:9; cf. 7:14).

referents.referent: Prominent martyrs and apostates of Antiochus's persecution

interpretations.label: Metaphorical: the Maccabean loyalists "rise" from caves to victory (Porphyry, via Jerome)
interpretations.framework: Anti-Christian philosophical critique (3rd century), known through Jerome
interpretations.summary: The persecution under Antiochus and Lysias was the unequalled trouble; after Antiochus died in Persia the faithful hidden in caves (1 Macc 2) rose "as if" from the dead to victory, while the apostates rose to disgrace. Jerome objects that Porphyry cannot say who "shone like the stars" and that the Babylonian catastrophe was greater.

title: A time, times and a half; 1,290 and 1,335 days (Dan 12:7, 11–12)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: The man in linen swears it will be "a time, times and a half"; from the removal of the continual offering and the setting up of the abomination there will be 1,290 days; blessed is the one who reaches 1,335 days. Arithmetic recorded (operator): 1,290 − 1,260 = 30; 1,335 − 1,290 = 45; 3½ years of 360 days = 1,260; 8:14's 2,300 offerings = 1,150 days.
in_text_interpretation: The text gives the starting point of the 1,290 days — the removal of the continual offering and the setting up of the abomination (cf. 11:31) — but not the end-point of either number; "a time, times and a half" also appears in 7:25.

interpretations.label: Day counts from the desecration of 15 Chislev 145 (Dec 168): 1,290 days to c. June 164, the death of Antiochus
proponents: C. H. Cornill (as cited by Driver: 6 June 164)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the starting point is the event of 11:31 (1 Macc 1:54). 1,290 days from Dec 168 end in June 164; Antiochus died in 164 (exact date unknown), and the writer may have pictured his death at that point; the further 45 days to 1,335 mark when blessedness would begin — "impossible to say with any certainty" (Driver). Objections: the Temple was rededicated after about 3 years and 10 days (1 Macc 4:52), not 1,290 days; the result depends on dating the desecration to 168 (disputed) and on an unknown date of death.

interpretations.label: Successive glosses lengthening the 1,150 days as the end was delayed
interpretations.summary: The 1,290 and the 1,335 days are "successive later insertions, due to the retardation of the term of 1150 days" (8:14); Montgomery notes general agreement on 168 and 165 for the desecration and rededication, and that Josephus's 3½ years (B.J.) accommodates Daniel while 1 Maccabees keeps three years. No fulfilment is claimed.

interpretations.label: Porphyry: 1,290 days of the desolation under Antiochus; 45 more days of victory and cleansing (via Jerome)
interpretations.framework: Anti-Christian philosophical critique (3rd century), known through Jerome
interpretations.summary: The 1,290 days were the desolation of the Temple under Antiochus; the extra 45 days were Judas Maccabaeus's victory over Antiochus's generals and the cleansing of the Temple. Jerome objects that 1 Maccabees and Josephus give three years, not three and a half.

interpretations.label: The Antichrist's 3½ years; 45 more days to Christ's coming / to the judgment of the nations
interpretations.summary: Jerome: the Antichrist persecutes 1,290 days and dies; the Lord comes in glory within the further 45 days. Guzik: 1,260 days to Christ's return, 1,290 to the installation of his government, 1,335 to the judgment of the nations (Matt 25:31–46); he admits the relationship is difficult. Future reference; not a claim of historical fulfilment.

referents.referent: The last 3½ years of the 70th week

interpretations.label: Year-day: 1,290 years from AD 508 to 1798; 1,335 years to AD 1843
interpretations.summary: A prophetic day is a year; the "daily" taken away is pagan worship, removed in AD 508; 1,290 years end in 1798 with the end of papal civil power; 1,335 years end in 1843 with Christ's return and the first resurrection. Objection: the expected return in 1843 did not occur; Guzik and Driver read the numbers as days.

interpretations.label: Symbolic numbers: a God-measured period of the affliction under Antiochus, not reckonable
interpretations.summary: The 1,290 days denote in general the sorest affliction of Israel by Antiochus — a moderate period exactly measured by God — and the extra 45 days a short further time until the oppression wholly ceases; neither number can be reckoned chronologically (both slightly exceed 3½ years of 360 days). Keil objects to the Antiochus-death reading: 2,300 evening-mornings are whole days, and no event 45 days after Antiochus's death began a better time — the war continued under Antiochus V (1 Macc 6:18–54) and the victory over Nicanor came two years later (1 Macc 7:26–50). Objection: Driver and Montgomery treat the numbers as calendar days (or glosses).

referents.referent: The God-measured time of affliction under Antiochus

title: Seal the book until the time of the end (Dan 12:4, 9)
speaker: The man clothed in linen
description: Daniel is to close and seal the book to the time of the end; many will run to and fro and knowledge will increase.
in_text_interpretation: 12:9 repeats that the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end, and 12:10 that the wise will understand.

interpretations.label: Many will read and search the obscure book
interpretations.summary: "Many shall pass through" = many will read the book and disagree about its fulfilment because of its obscurity (cf. Isa 29:11; Rev 5).

interpretations.label: End-time increase of prophetic knowledge (and, for some, travel and information)
proponents: D. Guzik (citing Wood and Newell; quoting Adam Clarke)
interpretations.summary: Guzik notes the common reading of modern travel and the information explosion, prefers "searching for knowledge", and suggests that the growth of prophetic study over the last 150 years indicates the period has begun. This is a tentative fulfilment claim about modern times.

title: The cup of the wine of wrath for the nations (Jer 25:15–38)
speaker: The LORD, through Jeremiah
description: Jeremiah is to make the nations drink the cup of wrath — Jerusalem and Judah first, then Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Sidon, Arabia, Elam, the Medes, all the kings of the north and all the kingdoms — and last "the king of Sheshach"; the LORD roars against all flesh.
in_text_interpretation: The text interprets the cup as the sword the LORD sends (25:16, 27) and begins with Jerusalem (25:18, 29). It does not explain Sheshach.

interpretations.label: Babylon's conquests of the listed nations in the sixth century, ending with Babylon's own fall
proponents: C. L. Feinberg (via Guzik): the "many nations and great kings" are the Medes and Persians
Josephus (Ant. 10.9.7) for the campaign against Ammon, Moab and Egypt in Nebuchadnezzar's 23rd year
interpretations.summary: Judah, its neighbours and Egypt fell under Nebuchadnezzar; Babylon itself fell to the Medes and Persians (cf. 25:12–14). Josephus reports a campaign of Nebuchadnezzar's 23rd year against Coele-Syria, Ammon, Moab and Egypt. Objection: Guzik judges the list too complete for one historical sequence.

referents.symbol: The king of Sheshach drinks last

interpretations.label: The final judgment of the nations
interpretations.summary: The list is too complete to fit one event; the ultimate fulfilment is the judgment of the nations (Rev 19:11–18). Not a historical fulfilment claim.

interpretations.label: Sheshach = Babel by atbash cipher
interpretations.summary: Reversing the alphabet turns ššk into bbl (Babel). Kidner notes Babylon is named openly elsewhere, so the code may reflect a habit of caution. An identification within the text, not a fulfilment claim.

title: Cyrus the LORD's shepherd and anointed (Isa 44:24–45:13)
speaker: The LORD (through the prophet)
description: The LORD names Cyrus "my shepherd", who will fulfil his purpose, say of Jerusalem "She will be built" and of the Temple "Your foundation will be laid" (44:28); calls him "his anointed", whose right hand he has held, to subdue nations and open doors and gates (45:1–3), for Israel's sake though Cyrus has not known him (45:4–5); he will build the LORD's city and free the exiles, not for price or reward (45:13).
in_text_interpretation: The text names Cyrus explicitly (44:28; 45:1) and states the purposes: Jerusalem rebuilt, the Temple founded, exiles freed. It does not name Babylon in these verses (cf. 47:1; 48:14).

interpretations.label: Predictive prophecy of Isaiah of Jerusalem, fulfilled by Cyrus (539–538)
proponents: Josephus (Ant. 11.1.1–2: Cyrus read his name in Isaiah, "one hundred and forty years before the temple was demolished")
D. Guzik (more than 200 years before Cyrus's birth; citing Poole and Motyer)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the book is headed as Isaiah's (1:1), and the passage presents the naming of Cyrus as proof that the LORD foretells (44:24–26). Fulfilment: Cyrus took Babylon (539) and in his first year authorised the return and the Temple (Ezra 1; 2 Chr 36:22–23). Guzik: the name is woven into the poem and cannot be a later insertion; Motyer: no basis to limit prediction. Josephus says Cyrus himself was moved by reading it. Objection: critical scholarship dates the passage to Cyrus's own career (below). Note: the Whiston text of Josephus gives 140 years before the destruction; Guzik (via Bultema) reports 220.

interpretations.label: An exilic prophet announcing Cyrus's imminent conquest (c. 546–539), fulfilled shortly after
proponents: J. Skinner (1898), summarising S. R. Driver
J. C. Döderlein (1775), with Ibn Ezra as a guarded forerunner (per Skinner)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: Cyrus is addressed as an already famous conqueror whose victories have shaken the world (41:2–3, 25) while Babylon's capture is still future (45:2–3; 48:14), so chs. 40–48 date between 550 and 539, almost certainly after the fall of Sardis (546); 46:1 may allude to Nabonidus's moving of the gods in 539 (Sellin, via Skinner). The announced events followed: Babylon fell in 539 and Cyrus's decree allowed the return. Objection: Guzik and Motyer reject the premise that detailed prediction is impossible; Skinner records that the case rests on internal evidence.
