title: King of Babylon

start_window.basis: ABC 5: Nabopolassar died 8 Abu (15 Aug 605) and Nebuchadnezzar took the throne on 1 Ululu (7 Sep 605); Julian equivalents per Parker & Dubberstein as given by Livius.

end_window.basis: Last tablet of Nebuchadnezzar and first of Amel-Marduk dated to the same day, 7 Oct 562 BC (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, via Wikipedia); one-week window.

notes: Model-independent reconstruction from the Babylonian chronicles and the stated reign lengths; individual chronologists differ by months.
title: King of Judah

start_window.basis: Josiah was killed as Necho marched north (2 Kgs 23:29); the Egyptian army crossed the Euphrates against Harran in Du'ûzu 609 and besieged it until Ulûlu (ABC 3); Jehoahaz reigned three months (2 Kgs 23:31) before Necho installed Jehoiakim (2 Kgs 23:34). Conservative window 1 Aug 609 – 31 Jan 608.

end_window.basis: Jehoiachin reigned three months (2 Kgs 24:8; "three months and ten days", 2 Chr 36:9) before Jerusalem was taken on 2 Addaru of Nebuchadnezzar's 7th year (ABC 5), i.e. 15/16 March 597; Jehoiakim's reign therefore ended roughly Nov 598 – Mar 597.

notes: Babylonian accession-year dating; reign length 17 years (accession year 556/555).
title: King of Babylon

start_window.basis: Between Neriglissar's last text (12 Apr 556) and the end of June 556, by which Nabonidus was sole ruler; his first dated texts are from 25 May 556 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, p. 11).

end_window.basis: Babylon fell on 16 Tašrītu of year 17 (ABC 7 iii 15) = 13 Oct 539 in Parker & Dubberstein (1942, p. 11); other modern conversions give 12 Oct. A Nabonidus-dated tablet from Uruk of the next day reflects delayed news.

notes: Cyrus's reign as king of Persia began c. 559 BC; this record covers only his rule over Babylon, which the Babylonian documents date by.
title: King of Babylon and of the lands (Babylonian dating)

start_window.basis: Babylonian texts date Cyrus from the fall of Babylon, 16 Tašrītu (13 Oct 539 in Parker & Dubberstein; 12 Oct in other conversions); his accession year runs to Nisan 538, and year 1 begins 1 Nisan = 24 Mar 538.

end_window.basis: Last Cyrus-dated tablets 12 Aug 530; first Cambyses tablet as sole king 31 Aug 530 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, p. 12).

notes: Parker & Dubberstein (1942, p. 21) note that Babylonian dates of Antiochus IV and Antiochus V cannot be separated; reign bounds here rest on the King List.
title: Seleucid king

start_window.basis: Accession in Ulûlu of Seleucid year 137 (BM 35603 rev. 9–10); Ulûlu of that year falls in August–September 175 BC (month-level; exact day not taken from the OCR tables).

end_window.basis: His death was reported in Babylon in Kislîmu of Seleucid year 148 (BM 35603 rev. 14); year 148 began 28 Mar 164 (Parker & Dubberstein), so Kislîmu ≈ late Nov – Dec 164. The death itself preceded the report; window opens 1 Sep 164. 1 Macc 6:16 gives year 149 on the Macedonian-reckoned era.

notes: A modelling device for Daniel 7:1 and 8:1 only.
title: Regent — "son of the king" with kingship entrusted (not a reign in Babylonian dating)

start_window.basis: Verse Account: the kingship was entrusted "when the third year was about to begin" (Livius ii 5–6); Smith (via Dougherty pp. 105–107) equates the Tema campaign with the Chronicle's 3rd year, whose western campaign runs Abu–Kislimu (ABC 7 i 11–17). Window: from the last quarter of year 2 (Ṭebētu began 10 Jan 553, Parker & Dubberstein) to the end of Kislimu year 3 (28 Dec 553). The breadth of the window is a modelling assumption.

end_window.basis: Assumes the regency lasted until the fall of Babylon (Dougherty's position); Nabonidus had returned to Babylon by his 17th year (ABC 7), so the delegated authority may have ended earlier.

notes: Babylonian (Nisan) reckoning: year 1 began 1 Nisan = 13 Apr 464; year 7 began 8 Apr 458; year 20 began 13 Apr 445 (Parker & Dubberstein table, p. 30). A Tishri-based Judean count is discussed under the Nehemiah event.
title: King of Persia (Babylonian dating)

start_window.basis: Aramaic papyrus Cowley 6 from Syene is dated 18 Kislev, "year 21, the accession year of Artaxerxes" (3 Jan 464); since Xerxes's year 21 had begun, Artaxerxes acceded after 1 Nisan 465 (Xerxes's month XII of year 20 ended 24 Mar 465) and before 3 Jan 464 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, p. 15).

end_window.basis: Last secure tablet of Artaxerxes I dated 12 Kislev year 41 (24 Dec 424); one tablet of 17 Shebat year 41 (26 Feb 423) may be a scribal error; Darius II recognised by mid-February 423 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, pp. 15–16).

notes: Year 1 began 1 Nisan 521 in Babylonian reckoning.
title: King of Persia (Babylonian dating)

start_window.basis: Bardiya killed by Darius on 10 Bagayadi (29 Sep 522; Behistun §13); first securely dated Babylonian tablet of Darius's accession year 20 Shebat (4 Feb 521, Sippar) (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, pp. 12–14). The Babylonian revolts of Nebuchadnezzar III and IV interrupted recognition in 522–521.

end_window.basis: Last dated tablets of Darius 19 Tashritu year 36 (30 Sep 486) and possibly 27 Arahsamnu (7 Nov 486); first tablet of Xerxes's accession year 22 Arahsamnu (1 Dec 486) (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, pp. 14–15).

notes: A reign of three months; no regnal-year statements depend on it.
title: King of Judah

start_window.basis: Three months (2 Kgs 24:8; "three months and ten days", 2 Chr 36:9) before the capture of 2 Adar year 7 (15/16 Mar 597, ABC 5); Wiseman (via Guzik) dates Jehoiakim's death about December 598. Window Nov–Dec 598 is an operator margin.

end_window.basis: Surrender at the capture of 2 Adar (15/16 Mar 597; ABC 5); 2 Chr 36:10 sends him to Babylon "at the turn of the year" (Nisan 597).

notes: End in summer 587 or 586 BC depending on reckoning (see the two chronology models).
title: King of Judah (vassal of Babylon)

start_window.basis: ABC 5: after capturing the city on 2 Adar year 7 (15/16 Mar 597) Nebuchadnezzar "appointed there a king of his own choice"; 2 Kgs 24:17. Upper bound (end of April 597) is an operator margin covering Nisan 597.

notes: Accession year Oct 562 – Mar 561; year 1 from 6 Apr 561 (Parker & Dubberstein table).
title: King of Babylon

start_window.basis: Last tablets of Nebuchadnezzar 25 Sep and 7 Oct 562 (Uruk); first tablet of Amel-Marduk's accession year 7 Oct 562 (Sippar?) (Parker & Dubberstein p. 10).

end_window.basis: Last tablet 7 Aug 560; first tablet of Nergal-shar-usur six days later (Parker & Dubberstein p. 10).

title: Carchemish: Nabopolassar year 21 (ABC 5) = Jehoiakim year 4 (Jer 46:2)
proposed_synchronization: Jeremiah 46:2 and the Babylonian Chronicle describe the same defeat of Necho II's army at Carchemish; the chronicle places it in Nabopolassar's 21st year, before his death on 8 Abu.
dating_method: Babylonian regnal year fixed to 605 BC by Ptolemy's Canon and astronomical texts (Parker & Dubberstein, via Livius)
assumptions: The Jeremiah superscription and the chronicle refer to one battle (both name Carchemish, Necho and Nebuchadnezzar).

window.basis: Narrated within Nabopolassar's 21st year (which began in Nisan 605, i.e. March/April) and before his death on 8 Abu = 15 Aug 605. Window starts 1 March for safety.

title: Capture of "the city of Judah" on 2 Addaru, Nebuchadnezzar year 7 (ABC 5) = Jehoiachin's surrender (2 Kgs 24:10–15)
proposed_synchronization: The chronicle's capture of the city of Judah and its king, and the installation of a king of Nebuchadnezzar's choice, correspond to Jehoiachin's surrender and Zedekiah's appointment.
dating_method: Babylonian date 2 Addaru, year 7 of Nebuchadnezzar = 15/16 March 597 BC (Parker & Dubberstein)
assumptions: "City of Judah" = Jerusalem; the unnamed king = Jehoiachin (identifications by the editors).

title: Jehoiakim year 4 = Nebuchadnezzar year 1 (Jer 25:1)
external_entity: Nebuchadnezzar II's regnal years (Babylonian, from ABC 5)
proposed_synchronization: Jeremiah 25:1 equates Jehoiakim's fourth year with Nebuchadnezzar's first; the Babylonian accession on 7 Sep 605 fixes Nebuchadnezzar's years.
dating_method: Nebuchadnezzar's accession year (Sep 605 – Nisan 604) and year 1 (Nisan 604 – Nisan 603)
assumptions: Whether Jeremiah counts Nebuchadnezzar's accession year as "first" is modelled as an alternative.

title: Fall of Babylon: 16 Tašrītu, Nabonidus year 17 (ABC 7)
proposed_synchronization: The Babylonian Chronicle dates the entry of Cyrus's army into Babylon to 16 Tašrītu of Nabonidus's 17th year; Daniel 5:28–31 places the end of Belshazzar's kingdom and its transfer to the Medes and Persians at that juncture.
dating_method: Babylonian day date converted with Parker & Dubberstein (1942) tables
assumptions: The chronicle year is lost on the tablet; the 17th year of Nabonidus is fixed by context and the Babylonian king-list chronology (Parker & Dubberstein).

window.basis: 16 Tašrītu year 17 = 13 Oct 539 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942, p. 11; month VII began 28 Sep). Many modern works give 12 Oct; the one-day spread reflects day-boundary and month-start conventions. Window 12–13 Oct.

title: Rededication: 25 Chislev 148 SE (1 Macc 4:52) = Dec 165 or Dec 164 BC
proposed_synchronization: The Seleucid date 25 Chislev 148 converts to December 165 BC on the Macedonian (autumn 312) epoch used by Driver and Montgomery, or to December 164 BC on a spring-311 epoch; Josephus's 154th Olympiad (Ol. 154.1 = 164/163 on the standard epoch, operator calculation) favours 164.
dating_method: Seleucid-era date; epoch of 1 Maccabees' reckoning disputed
assumptions: The two Seleucid-era epochs in 1 Maccabees are not resolved here; the window deliberately spans both.
Olympiad conversion (Ol. 1 = 776 BC) is an operator calculation, not a source statement.

window.basis: Covers Chislev under both Seleucid-era epochs: from mid-Nov 165 BC to mid-Jan 163 BC. Driver (p. 119) and Montgomery give Dec 165; Josephus's Olympiad points to Dec 164.

title: Battle of Raphia dated to 217 BC
proposed_synchronization: The battle took place in the campaigning season of 217 BC (Driver, from Polybius).
dating_method: Polybius's narrative chronology as dated by Driver
assumptions: Year from Driver ("in the next spring (217)"); Polybius's Olympiad reckoning not converted here.

title: Battle of Panium, c. 200–198 BC
proposed_synchronization: Antiochus III defeated Scopas at Paneion; Driver dates the decisive defeat and Scopas's surrender to 198 BC; Scopas was sent out in 200.
assumptions: Range 200–198 kept because the battle and the siege of Sidon are dated differently in the literature (only Driver read).

title: Battle of Magnesia, autumn 190 BC
proposed_synchronization: Driver dates the battle to the autumn of 190 BC.
assumptions: Livy not read directly; Appian's fetched section does not state the year.

title: Death of Seleucus IV: 10 Ululu, Seleucid year 137 (175 BC)
proposed_synchronization: Seleucus IV died on 10 Ululu 137 SE, the same month in which Antiochus IV ascended; Ululu 137 falls in Aug–Sep 175 BC.
dating_method: Babylonian king list, Seleucid era (Babylonian reckoning)

window.basis: Ululu of SE 137 (Babylonian epoch) = Aug–Sep 175 BC, as for the Antiochus IV reign record.

title: Popillius Laenas at Eleusis, 168 BC
proposed_synchronization: The meeting at Eleusis near Alexandria followed Rome's victory over Perseus (Pydna) in 168 BC (Driver).
dating_method: Driver's dating of Polybius and Livy

title: Desecration: 15 Chislev 145 SE (1 Macc 1:54) = Dec 168 or Dec 167 BC
proposed_synchronization: Chislev 145 SE is December 168 BC on the Macedonian (autumn 312) epoch used by Driver and Montgomery, or December 167 BC on a spring-311 epoch.
dating_method: Seleucid-era date; epoch of 1 Maccabees' reckoning disputed
assumptions: The window deliberately spans both Seleucid-era epochs, as for the rededication.

window.basis: Covers Chislev under both Seleucid-era epochs (mid-Nov 168 – mid-Jan 166 BC). Montgomery: "profanation Chislev 145 = 168".

title: Death of Antiochus IV reported in Babylon, Kislimu 148 SE (164 BC)
proposed_synchronization: The king list records that the death was heard in Kislimu of SE 148 (Nov–Dec 164 BC); Polybius places it at Tabae.
dating_method: Babylonian king list, Seleucid era (Babylonian reckoning)

window.basis: As for the end of the Antiochus IV reign record: news reached Babylon in Kislimu 148 (≈ late Nov – Dec 164); the death itself preceded the report.

symbols.symbol: Feet of iron and clay
symbols.description: Feet and toes
symbols.in_text_interpretation: A divided kingdom, partly strong and partly brittle; they will "mingle themselves with the seed of men" but not hold together (2:41–43).

symbols.symbol: Stone cut out without hands
symbols.description: Strikes the feet and becomes a great mountain
symbols.in_text_interpretation: A kingdom set up by the God of heaven "in the days of those kings", never to be destroyed (2:44–45).

description: A dream image: a great statue with head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with clay; a stone cut out without hands strikes the feet, the statue is shattered, and the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth.

title: The great tree cut down (Nebuchadnezzar's second dream)

symbols.symbol: The great tree
symbols.description: Reaches the sky, visible to the ends of the earth; shelter and food for all
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Nebuchadnezzar: "it is you, O king" (4:22).

symbols.symbol: The holy watcher
symbols.description: A heavenly figure who decrees the felling
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The decree of the watchers / the Most High (4:17, 24).

symbols.symbol: Stump bound with iron and bronze
symbols.description: Roots left in the earth
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The kingdom will be restored after he acknowledges Heaven's rule (4:26).

symbols.symbol: Seven times
symbols.description: Period passing over the one with an animal's heart
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The king's period of exclusion until he knows that the Most High rules (4:25, 32).

description: A tree at the centre of the earth reaching to the sky, sheltering beasts and birds, is ordered cut down by a holy watcher; the stump is left bound with iron and bronze, and "seven times" pass over him.

title: The four beasts, the Ancient of Days and one like a son of man (Dan 7)

symbols.symbol: Four winds stirring the great sea
symbols.description: The winds of heaven break out on the great sea
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The beasts "arise out of the earth" (7:17); the sea itself is not explained.

symbols.symbol: Lion with eagle's wings
symbols.description: Wings plucked; made to stand like a man and given a human heart
symbols.in_text_interpretation: One of four kings/kingdoms (7:17); not named in Dan 7.

symbols.symbol: Bear raised on one side with three ribs
symbols.description: Told to devour much flesh
symbols.in_text_interpretation: One of four kings/kingdoms (7:17); not named.

symbols.symbol: Leopard with four wings and four heads
symbols.description: Dominion was given to it
symbols.in_text_interpretation: One of four kings/kingdoms (7:17); not named.

symbols.symbol: Fourth beast with iron teeth
symbols.description: Devours, crushes and tramples; different from the others
symbols.in_text_interpretation: A fourth kingdom, different from all the others, that will devour the whole earth (7:23); not named.

symbols.symbol: Ten horns
symbols.description: On the fourth beast
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Ten kings arising from the fourth kingdom (7:24); not named.

symbols.symbol: Little horn
symbols.description: Rises among the ten, uproots three, has human eyes and an arrogant mouth, makes war on the saints
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Another king, different from the former, who puts down three kings, speaks against the Most High, wears out the saints and plans to change times and law, for "a time and times and half a time" (7:24–25); not named.

symbols.symbol: Thrones and the Ancient of Days
symbols.description: White clothing, hair like wool, a fiery throne with burning wheels
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Not explicitly identified; he judges and gives judgment for the saints (7:22).

symbols.symbol: Fiery stream, myriads, the court and the books
symbols.description: Judgment is set and books are opened
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The judgment that takes away the horn's dominion (7:26).

symbols.symbol: The beast slain and burned; other beasts' lives prolonged
symbols.description: Dominion removed
symbols.in_text_interpretation: The fourth kingdom's end (7:26); the others are not explained.

symbols.symbol: One like a son of man with the clouds
symbols.description: Brought to the Ancient of Days and given everlasting dominion
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Not explicitly identified; the interpretation gives the everlasting kingdom to "the saints of the Most High" (7:18, 22, 27).

description: Night vision of beasts from the sea, a heavenly court, and a human-like figure receiving an everlasting kingdom, followed by an interpretation from an attendant. Identifications below are only those the text makes; all others are interpretations recorded on the prophecy records.

title: The ram and the goat (Dan 8)

symbols.symbol: Ram with two horns, the higher coming up last
symbols.description: Pushes west, north and south
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "The kings of Media and Persia" (8:20).

symbols.symbol: Male goat from the west, not touching the ground
symbols.description: Breaks the ram's two horns
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "The king of Greece" (8:21).

symbols.symbol: Great horn between the goat's eyes, broken at its height
symbols.description: Replaced by four horns
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "The first king" of Greece (8:21); not named.

symbols.symbol: Four notable horns toward the four winds
symbols.description: Rise in place of the great horn
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "Four kingdoms will stand up out of the nation, but not with his power" (8:22); not named.

symbols.symbol: Little horn from one of the four
symbols.description: Grows toward the south, the east and the glorious land; casts down host and stars; removes the continual offering; casts down the sanctuary
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "A king of fierce face" in the latter time of their kingdom (8:23–25); not named.

symbols.symbol: The prince of the host
symbols.description: Against whom the horn magnifies itself
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "The prince of princes" (8:25); not further identified.

symbols.symbol: 2,300 evenings and mornings
symbols.description: Until the sanctuary is cleansed
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "The vision of the evenings and mornings … is true" and belongs to many days to come (8:26); the unit is not explained.

description: A ram, a goat, four horns and a little horn that attacks the host of heaven and the sanctuary, interpreted by Gabriel. Unlike ch. 7, the text itself names Media, Persia and Greece; later identifications (Alexander, the successors, Antiochus) are interpretations recorded on the prophecy records.

title: The vision by the Tigris (Dan 10–12)

symbols.symbol: A man clothed in linen, girded with gold of Uphaz
symbols.description: Body like beryl, face like lightning, eyes like torches, arms and feet like bronze, voice like a multitude
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Not named. He says he was "sent" (10:11); reappears above the river in 12:6–7.

symbols.symbol: One in the likeness of the sons of men
symbols.description: Touches Daniel's lips and strengthens him
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Not named; whether the same as the man in linen is not stated.

symbols.symbol: The prince of the kingdom of Persia
symbols.description: Withstands the speaker 21 days
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Called a "prince" (sar); his nature is not explained.

symbols.symbol: Michael, one of the chief princes
symbols.description: Comes to help the speaker
symbols.in_text_interpretation: "Michael your prince" (10:21); "the great prince who stands for the children of your people" (12:1).

symbols.symbol: The prince of Greece
symbols.description: Will come when the speaker goes out
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Not explained.

symbols.symbol: The writing of truth
symbols.description: Source of what the speaker will reveal
symbols.in_text_interpretation: Not explained.

description: The last vision of Daniel, received by the Tigris in Cyrus's third year. Chapter 10 is the frame: a heavenly figure and a conflict of heavenly "princes". The revelation proper (11:2–12:4) and the closing dialogue (12:5–13) are recorded with chapters 11 and 12.
